title: Seawanhacky / Sewanhaka
summary: Seawanhacky, also Sewanhaka, is a name for Long Island found in Dutch-period purchase documents.
history_content: The earliest cited records are three 1636 Indian deeds for meadows at what is now Flatlands, Brooklyn, describing the island as Sewanhacky or Sewanhacking. The name is not found in early eastern Long Island records.
translation_content:
Seawanhacky is interpreted as "the sewan country," connecting sewan or seawan with wampum or shell-money, and -hacky or -hacking with land or country.

Why Place Names Matter

“Place names, as cultural heritage, include significant regional, geographic, and socio-historical information.”

— Li Zhang, Sifan Zhou, and Junwei Ren, Spatiotemporal distribution of toponymic cultural heritage of water-related settlement place names in Manas River Basin (2025), Abstract
preservation_content: Seawanhacky connects Long Island with wampum, shell-bead production, and early Dutch records. It also shows how Native names for the island competed with names preferred by European mapmakers.
